observations.observed: The image shows an AP abdominal aortogram. The contrast-opacified aorta courses centrally with normal calibre at the level of the renal arteries; bilateral renal arteries arise and supply normally enhancing kidneys. Infrarenal to the renal ostia, a focal aneurysmal dilatation approximately twice the suprarenal aortic width is visible, bulging predominantly to the patient's left. Below the aneurysm sac the aorta reconstitutes and bifurcates into bilateral common iliac arteries without further aneurysmal change. Lumbar and mesenteric branch vessels are opacified. No contrast extravasation outside the vessel lumen is identified.

observations.observed: The projection is AP, the anatomy is abdominal aorta and its branches, consistent with an aortogram. The bony structures visible (lumbar spine, pelvis) show skeletally mature appearances appropriate for an adult over 60. No anatomical impossibility is identified.

findings: Anteroposterior projection catheter-based contrast aortogram or CT angiogram maximum-intensity-projection image of the abdominal aorta and its branches

Focal saccular to fusiform dilation of the infrarenal abdominal aorta, approximately two to three times the diameter of the suprarenal aorta, consistent with an infrarenal aortic aneurysm; the aneurysm sac appears to extend below the renal artery origins and above the aortic bifurcation
Bilateral renal arteries are opacified and appear patent with visible intrarenal branching; both kidneys are visible as soft-tissue density structures
Celiac axis and superior mesenteric artery origins are suggested in the upper abdomen; inferior mesenteric artery branches are visible arising from the lower aneurysm segment
Aortic bifurcation into bilateral common iliac arteries is visualized; iliac vessels appear patent without obvious additional aneurysmal dilation
Bony pelvis and lumbar spine are visible in the background; no calcification or bony destruction is noted
differential: Infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), atherosclerotic in etiology — most likely given the location, morphology, and infrarenal position sparing the renal artery origins
Inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm — cannot be excluded on this image alone; periaortic soft tissue thickening would require cross-sectional imaging to assess
Mycotic (infectious) aortic aneurysm — saccular morphology could suggest this; clinical correlation required
anatomyConcerns: The aneurysmal segment appears to involve the infrarenal aorta below the renal artery origins, which is anatomically consistent; however, precise relationship to the renal arteries and iliac bifurcation should be confirmed on cross-sectional imaging for surgical planning
No obvious filling defect suggestive of intraluminal thrombus is visible on this projection, but mural thrombus can obscure on single-plane angiography
Asymmetry in renal size is noted with the right kidney appearing larger than the left; clinical significance uncertain without additional views

imageApproval.diagnosticReason: The aortogram demonstrates a focal infrarenal aneurysmal dilatation of the abdominal aorta below the renal artery origins, with the sac approximately twice the suprarenal aortic diameter, tapering back to a normal calibre bifurcation. Both renal arteries are patent with normal parenchymal enhancement. The infrarenal location, fusiform-to-saccular morphology, and clinical context of a dull lower back ache in an older adult together strongly favour atherosclerotic infrarenal AAA over inflammatory or mycotic subtypes, which would require additional cross-sectional features not visible here. The asymmetry in renal size is a projected appearance difference and does not constitute an independent lesion. The aneurysm bulge is predominantly leftward as expected.
